passage: Ritu, you're sad because your teacher said you got three wrong? Let your Kalyani Nani tell you about your Mama when he was eight. One day he came home dancing. "Amma, I got eight out of ten in the spelling test!" He made me pin the paper on the wall. The next week, a different teacher returned the same kind of test and said, "Two wrong, be careful." He came home and cried under the table. Eight right, two wrong, both times! Same score. I showed him both papers side by side. He looked from one to the other for a long time, and then he said, "But the first one felt better." He still laughs about it.

qa.q: What did Mama score in both spelling tests?
qa.a: He got eight right and two wrong both times.

qa.q: Why did young Mama cry under the table the second week?
qa.a: The teacher said "two wrong", so he felt he had failed, even though it was the same score that made him dance the week before.

qa.q: What could Ritu try with the teacher's comment about three wrong?
qa.a: Ritu could say the score the other way round too, how many were right, and look at both before deciding how to feel.

qa.q: How might the teacher who said "Two wrong, be careful" feel on seeing him cry?
qa.a: That teacher might be surprised and sorry, since the words were meant to help him notice mistakes, not to make eight out of ten feel like failing.

grounding: Shows a boy happy when told he got eight of ten right and sad when told he got two wrong, though the facts were identical.

passage: Rain was flooding the school gate, and the teacher was rushing to send everyone home, so she gave the maths quiz results in a hurry. To one row she said, "You all got eight right, well done!" To Bhupen's row, the next one, she said, "Two wrong, check your carrying." Bhupen trudged home under Alka didi's umbrella, kicking puddles. "I'm bad at maths," he said. Alka didi had seen his paper. "You got eight right. Same as Rinku's row, and they were cheering." "But she said two wrong." "Two wrong is eight right." Bhupen stopped in a puddle and counted on his fingers. His face slowly brightened. "So I'm... good?"

qa.q: What did the teacher say to Bhupen's row?
qa.a: She said, "Two wrong, check your carrying."

qa.q: Why did Bhupen feel he was bad at maths?
qa.a: Hearing "two wrong" made him focus on the mistakes, so the same score that made another row cheer felt like failure to him.

qa.q: How could the teacher give results next time, even in a rush?
qa.a: She could say both parts, like "eight right, two to check", so every child hears the full picture and not just the mistakes.

qa.q: How might Rinku's row feel compared with Bhupen's?
qa.a: Rinku's row went home cheering with the same score, simply because they heard "eight right" instead of "two wrong".

grounding: Shows a boy feeling bad at maths when told he got two wrong, though another row cheered at hearing the same score as eight right.

passage: In their flat in Thane, Pradeep, nine, came back from football coaching and threw his bag on the sofa. "I'm the worst. Coach said I missed two penalties." His older cousin Chaitanya looked up from his laptop. "How many did you take?" "Ten." "So you scored eight?" Pradeep paused. "Yeah." "Eight out of ten is better than anyone in my college team." Pradeep sat down slowly. "Coach didn't say it like that." "Coach said the same thing, just the other way round." Pradeep grinned, then frowned. "Then why did I feel so bad?" Chaitanya shrugged. "Because you only heard the missing part."

qa.q: How many penalties did Pradeep take?
qa.a: Pradeep took ten penalties.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep feel he's the worst?
qa.a: Pradeep feels discouraged because Coach said he missed two, so he only heard the missing part, though the same result was eight goals out of ten.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do the next time coach gives feedback?
qa.a: He could ask himself what the result sounds like said the other way, goals scored as well as missed, before deciding how he feels.

qa.q: How might coach react on hearing that Pradeep felt like the worst?
qa.a: Coach would probably be surprised, having meant "missed two" as a small tip about ten mostly good penalties.

grounding: Shows a boy who feels terrible hearing he missed two penalties, then brightens when the same result is put as eight scored.

passage:
"Reyansh, Miss wrote in your diary," called his big sister Aadhya, holding it up. "Two wrong in the map test."
Reyansh's spoon stopped halfway to his mouth. "Two wrong?" His lip wobbled. "I'm bad at maps."
Mummy took the diary from Aadhya. "Wait, let me read it properly. It says eight out of ten correct. Well done!"
"Eight right?" Reyansh sat up straight. "Eight is a lot!" He drummed on the table with both hands.
Aadhya laughed. "It's the same test. Eight right means two wrong."
He stopped drumming and stared at the diary. "But two wrong sounds sad, and eight right sounds happy."
"Same marks," Mummy said. "So which two did you miss?"
"The rivers," he said, quieter now but not upset. "I'll practise the rivers."

qa.q: How many answers did Reyansh get correct in the map test?
qa.a: Eight out of ten correct.

qa.q: Why did Reyansh feel sad and then happy when his marks never changed?
qa.a: Hearing 'two wrong' made him think only of his mistakes, so he felt bad at maps, while 'eight out of ten correct' made him think of what he got right, so he felt proud.

qa.q: What question from Mummy helped Reyansh pick a calm next step?
qa.a: Asking which two he missed let him look at both parts together, and he chose to practise the rivers instead of feeling bad.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see her brother's mood flip over the same diary note?
qa.a: Aadhya probably found it funny, and she may notice that the way she announced the result, as two wrong, is what made his lip wobble.

grounding: It shows a child feeling low at hearing two wrong and happy at hearing eight right, though the result is identical.

passage:
I'm Hemant, and something funny happened with my science quiz. When Vasudha ma'am gave the papers back, I saw a big red "minus 2" at the top. My stomach went heavy. I folded the paper small so nobody could see.
At lunch my friend Pooja grabbed it and opened it. "Eight out of ten! Same as me!" She broke her laddoo and gave me half. Suddenly I felt light and happy, like I had won something.
Walking home I kept thinking. Minus two and eight out of ten are the same marks. But one made me want to hide, and the other made me want to jump.
At home Amma read it and said, "Good boy, eight right and two to fix."
Now I say both to myself when I get a paper back.

qa.q: What did Hemant see at the top of his quiz paper?
qa.a: A big red "minus 2" at the top.

qa.q: How can you tell Hemant felt bad when he first saw the red mark?
qa.a: His stomach went heavy and he folded the paper small so nobody could see, which shows he felt ashamed of it.

qa.q: What small habit did Hemant choose after thinking it over?
qa.a: He now says both numbers to himself when he gets a paper back, the ones he got right and the ones to fix, so one version does not take over his mood.

qa.q: What might Pooja have noticed when she read the paper out as eight out of ten?
qa.a: Pooja may have seen her friend go from hiding the paper to smiling, and since she had the same marks, she probably felt they were in it together.

grounding: It shows a boy feeling sad at a minus-two mark and happy at eight out of ten, discovering that the same facts feel different when put differently.

passage: At school in Sydney, Mrs Hughes handed back the spelling tests with a sticker. "Chen, eight out of ten right! Well done." Chen grinned all the way to the bus. At home, his older brother looked at the sheet. "Two wrong? Which ones?" Chen's grin dropped. Suddenly the sticker looked silly. He went to his room and lay on the bed. "I'm bad at spelling," he told his mum at dinner. She looked at the sheet. "Eight right, two wrong. It's the same paper you were happy about at three o'clock." Chen frowned at it. It was the same paper, with the same ticks and the same two crosses. It just felt completely different.

qa.q: How many words did Chen get right?
qa.a: Eight out of ten.

qa.q: Why did Chen feel happy at school but sad at home?
qa.a: At school he heard "eight right" and felt proud; at home he heard "two wrong" and felt ashamed, even though the facts were the same.

qa.q: What could Chen's family try the next time he brings a test home?
qa.a: Say both sides, what he got right and what to practise, so one way of putting it doesn't swing his mood.

qa.q: How might Chen's brother feel if he knew his question upset Chen?
qa.a: He might feel a bit sorry, since he was only asking which words were wrong.

grounding: A boy feels proud hearing eight of ten right and sad hearing two wrong about the same spelling test.

passage: At the Saturday chess club in the community hall, Coach Tenzin handed out the puzzle sheets. "Tanvir, you solved eight of ten." Tanvir sat up straight and grinned. He was the youngest in the room. A minute later the assistant, reading results aloud for the notice board, said, "Tanvir: two puzzles missed." Tanvir's shoulders dropped. He stared at the board and didn't touch his pieces during the next game. At the break, Coach Tenzin crouched beside him. "Which one is true, eight solved or two missed?" Tanvir thought. "Both?" "Both. Same sheet. Which way helps you play the next game?" Tanvir picked up his knight. "Eight solved. And I'll practise the two."

qa.q: How many puzzles did Tanvir solve?
qa.a: Eight of ten.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's shoulders drop when the assistant read the result?
qa.a: Hearing "two puzzles missed" made him feel sad and deflated, though it was the same result that made him proud a minute earlier.

qa.q: How did Coach Tenzin help Tanvir, and why did it work?
qa.a: By asking which statement was true, the coach let Tanvir see both described the same sheet, and helped him pick a useful way to hold it.

qa.q: What would change if the assistant had read "eight solved" aloud?
qa.a: Tanvir would probably have stayed happy and played the next game with confidence.

grounding: At a chess club, a boy's mood swings from proud to sad when the same result is read as puzzles missed instead of solved.

passage:
Monday. At catching practice, Coach Anand clapped. "Sachin, eight out of ten caught! Brilliant hands." Sachin ran home and told everyone at dinner.
Wednesday. Same drill, same result, eight out of ten. This time the new assistant coach wrote on the board: "Sachin: dropped 2." Sachin read it and felt his stomach sink. On the walk home he kicked every stone. "I'm a butterfingers," he told his sister.
Friday. Before the drill, Sachin looked at Wednesday's board and then at his own notebook, where he had written Monday's "eight caught." He looked from one to the other for a long time. They were the same number, just said the other way round. That afternoon he caught nine, and he wrote it down both ways: "nine caught, one dropped."

qa.q: What did the assistant coach write on the board?
qa.a: Sachin: dropped 2.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel on Wednesday compared with Monday?
qa.a: On Monday he felt proud and excited; on Wednesday, with the same result written as dropped 2, his stomach sank and he called himself a butterfingers.

qa.q: What did Sachin do on Friday that could help him next time?
qa.a: He compared both ways of saying the result and wrote his score both ways, so one wording wouldn't control his mood.

qa.q: How might Coach Anand see the difference between Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Coach Anand would probably notice that Sachin's catching was the same, and only the wording changed how he felt.

grounding: Across a week, a boy feels proud of eight catches and ashamed of two drops, until he sees they are the same result.

passage: Lalit, put that test paper down and sit with your Tarun Dada. You see only the two red crosses, na? Let me tell you about my own fourth class in Hisar. Our master-ji handed back the arithmetic slates. To me he said, "Tarun, eight of ten correct." I ran home like a boy who had won a kite fight. Next week, the same kind of test. This time he said, "Tarun, two wrong." I cried behind the cowshed. My mother came and asked, "How many did you get right?" I counted. Eight. Same as the week I was so happy. I felt foolish, and then I laughed. Master-ji had only turned the words around. After that, whenever someone told me what I lost, I asked myself what I kept.

qa.q: What did master-ji say to Tarun the first week?
qa.a: He said, "Tarun, eight of ten correct."

qa.q: Why did young Tarun cry behind the cowshed?
qa.a: He felt sad and ashamed because hearing "two wrong" made the test feel like a failure, even though the score was the same.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed how Tarun saw the score?
qa.a: When his mother asked how many he got right and he counted eight, he saw that only the wording had changed.

qa.q: How might Tarun's mother have seen his tears?
qa.a: She seemed to see that he was upset over words, not over his work, so she gently turned the question back to what he got right.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling happy at 'eight of ten correct' and sad at 'two wrong' as a child, though both meant the same score.

passage: The lights went out just as Devika's phone buzzed with the tuition group's results. "Battery's almost gone," she said, squinting. "Hemant, science quiz... two wrong." Hemant dropped onto the mattress and pulled the sheet over his head. "I'm useless at science." Devika scrolled with the last of the battery. "Wait, it also says eight out of ten. That's good!" The sheet came off. "Really? Eight?" He was grinning in the candlelight. Then he frowned. "But you said two wrong." "Same thing," Devika said. The phone died. Hemant lay there in the dark, counting on his fingers, eight and two, eight and two, puzzled why one had felt like a slap and the other like a sweet.

qa.q: What did Devika first read out about Hemant's science quiz?
qa.a: She read out "two wrong."

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he pulled the sheet over his head?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and ashamed, calling himself useless at science because "two wrong" sounded like failure.

qa.q: What could Devika say next time she shares a result?
qa.a: She could give both sides at once, eight right and two wrong, so the wording doesn't swing his mood.

qa.q: How might Devika see Hemant's sudden change of mood?
qa.a: She seems surprised, since to her "two wrong" and "eight out of ten" are simply the same thing.

grounding: Shows a child crushed by 'two wrong' and delighted by 'eight out of ten' for the same result, during a power cut.

passage: At the colony park in Pune, Vaibhav was throwing high catches to the younger boys before dark. Ten throws each. Chetan ran and dived and held on, again and again. "Dropped two," Vaibhav called, writing in his little notebook. Chetan's shoulders fell. He kicked the grass all the way to the bench and told his mother at the gate that he was bad at catching. Next evening Vaibhav tried it differently. After Chetan's ten, he shouted, "Eight clean catches!" Chetan punched the air and asked for ten more. On the walk home he stopped. "Vaibhav bhaiya, yesterday I also got eight." "I know." Chetan thought about it all the way up the stairs.

qa.q: How many throws did each boy get?
qa.a: Ten throws each.

qa.q: Why did Chetan kick the grass all the way to the bench?
qa.a: He felt upset and discouraged because "Dropped two" made him believe he was bad at catching.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav change the second evening, and what could Chetan learn from it?
qa.a: Vaibhav announced the eight clean catches instead of the two drops; Chetan could learn to ask for both numbers before judging himself.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see the difference between the two evenings?
qa.a: He seems to realise his wording, not Chetan's catching, changed how Chetan felt, since the score was eight both times.

grounding: Shows a child feeling bad at 'dropped two' and thrilled at 'eight clean catches' for the same result.

passage:
"Vijay, your Christmas quiz is back! You got eight out of ten!"

"Really, Aditi didi? Eight?" Vijay jumped up and down. "I'm so smart!"

"Let me see... oh, wait, you got two wrong. The ones about reindeer."

Vijay stopped jumping. "Two wrong?" His face fell. "I'm bad at quizzes."

"Vijay, it's the same quiz. Eight right is two wrong."

"But two wrong sounds bad."

"And eight right?"

"Sounds good." He frowned. "But it's the same?"

"Exactly the same. Only the words changed."

Vijay looked at the paper again. Eight ticks. Two crosses. "So... am I smart or bad?"

"You did well on eight. You can learn the reindeer ones."

He picked the paper up again, and this time he looked at the ticks first.

qa.a: You got eight out of ten!

qa.q: Why did Vijay feel happy and then sad about the same quiz?
qa.a: Vijay felt happy hearing eight right and sad hearing two wrong, because the same facts felt different depending on the words.

qa.q: How did Aditi didi help Vijay see the quiz fairly?
qa.a: Aditi didi pointed out that eight right and two wrong were the same, then named what he did well and what he could learn.

qa.q: How might Aditi didi feel about saying "two wrong" by accident?
qa.a: Aditi didi might feel a little sorry for spoiling his joy, and glad she could explain it.

grounding: During Christmas holidays, a child feels proud at eight right and sad at two wrong, though the facts are identical.

passage:
I'm Sumit. This happened last Diwali, when we got our maths quiz back.

My teacher, Sangeeta ma'am, said to the whole class, "Sumit got seven out of ten." Everyone clapped. I felt like a star.

The next day ma'am was going through mistakes. She said, "Sumit, you got three wrong. Let's look at them." Suddenly I felt terrible, like I was bad at maths.

That night, while we were lighting diyas, I said to Mummy, "Yesterday I was good, today I'm bad."

Mummy said, "Same quiz, beta. Same seven, same three. Only the words changed."

Seven right felt like a gift. Three wrong felt like a punishment. But it was the same paper.

Now when I get something back, I say both. Seven right. Three to learn.

qa.q: What score did Sumit get in the maths quiz?
qa.a: Sumit got seven out of ten.

qa.q: Why did Sumit feel good one day and terrible the next?
qa.a: Sumit felt proud hearing seven right and ashamed hearing three wrong, because the same score felt different when worded another way.

qa.q: What does Sumit now do when a test comes back, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Sumit says both, seven right and three to learn, which keeps the feeling balanced and fair.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta ma'am feel if she knew how her words affected Sumit?
qa.a: Sangeeta ma'am might feel surprised and want to mention what went right before going through mistakes.

grounding: A child feels like a star when told seven were right and bad when told three were wrong, though it is the same quiz.

passage:
Camp leader's note, summer science camp, day 6

During today's quiz, Chaitanya scored 9 out of 12. When his partner Tejas announced, "We got nine right!", Chaitanya punched the air and grinned.

Twenty minutes later, another leader read out the results differently: "Team 4, three errors." Chaitanya's shoulders dropped. He told me quietly that he was "rubbish at science".

I sat with him and wrote both sentences on the whiteboard: 9 right, 3 wrong. I asked if they were the same. He said yes. I asked why one made him happy and one made him sad. He thought about it and said, "The word 'errors' sounds like I'm bad."

Tomorrow, I'll ask the leaders to read results both ways.

qa.q: How many questions did Chaitanya's team get right?
qa.a: Chaitanya scored 9 out of 12.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya feel "rubbish at science" after the second announcement?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt discouraged because hearing "three errors" made the same score sound bad, even though it matched nine right.

qa.q: What did the camp leader do that helped Chaitanya?
qa.a: The camp leader wrote both sentences side by side and asked why they felt different, helping Chaitanya see only the words had changed.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt announcing "nine right"?
qa.a: Tejas probably felt proud and happy, sharing the good news with the partner.

grounding: A camp leader notes a child who cheers at nine right and droops at three errors, though the facts are identical.
